# Preface {.unnumbered}

Welcome to the **AI Engineering Handbook**: a from-scratch, proof-driven,
hands-on path that takes you from *"I have never written a program"* to
*"I can design, build, train, evaluate and ship intelligent systems"*.

The handbook follows, course by course, the topics of the twelve courses of the Master in
AI Engineering that I attended. For each course I wrote a
part of this book that is **far more detailed than the lectures**: every idea
is traced back to the book, paper or standard where it was born, every formula
is derived or proved, and every concept is illustrated with worked examples
and runnable code. Each part ends with the **final project** of the course,
which you can find, fully implemented, in the companion repository
[`matteo-zirilli/ai-projects`](https://github.com/matteo-zirilli/ai-projects).

## Who this book is for {.unnumbered}

The book assumes **no prior knowledge** of programming, machine learning or
advanced mathematics. What you need is curiosity and a computer. Whenever a
concept depends on another one, the dependency is either explained on the spot
or linked explicitly. If you already know some of the material, the
**learning objectives** at the top of each chapter tell you quickly whether you
can skip it.

## What makes this book different {.unnumbered}

1. **Nothing is taken for granted.** We do not say "a list append costs $O(1)$";
   we define what $O(\cdot)$ means, show how a list is laid out in memory, and
   *prove* that appending costs $O(1)$ on average.
2. **Every formula has a story.** For each result you will find *who* proposed
   it, *why* (what problem they were trying to solve), and *where* (the exact
   publication, with a reference you can look up).
3. **Two layers, one page.** Each page separates the **essentials** — what
   you must understand — from the **deep dives**: proofs, history, internals,
   extra code. Deep dives sit exactly where they belong in the text, as
   coloured bars you can open one by one; a **reading-mode switch**
   (*Essentials* / *Full*) opens or closes them all. See
   [Two reading modes](how-to-study.qmd#sec-reading-modes).
4. **Many examples.** Each idea is shown at least three ways: an intuition
   (an everyday analogy), a worked example by hand, and running code.
5. **Interactive widgets.** Some chapters contain small simulations that run
   in your browser (for instance, to see the exact bits of a floating-point
   number or how a hash table fills up). Move the sliders and watch the theory
   change in front of you.
6. **Verifiable references.** Every chapter ends with an annotated reading
   list, and @sec-finding-sources explains, step by step, how to find
   and read each kind of source (books, papers, standards, PEPs,
   documentation).

## Structure of the book {.unnumbered}

Each course of the master becomes a **part** of the book. The structure of
each part is always the same:

- an **overview page** with what you will be able to do, the map of the chapters,
  and the final project;
- one **chapter per topic** of the course, in which theory and practice are
  merged: ideas first, then runnable code;
- a **project chapter** that states the project requirements in my own words,
  maps each requirement to the chapters that teach the necessary skills, and
  walks through the design and implementation.

| Part | Course | Status |
|---|---|---|
| I | [Programming with Python](python/index.qmd) | ✅ available |
| II | [High-performance programming with C and C++](cpp/index.qmd) | ✅ available |
| III | [Foundations of machine learning](ml/index.qmd) | ✅ available |
| IV–XII | the remaining courses of the master | 🛠 in preparation |

## Conventions {.unnumbered}

The conventions used throughout the book (notation, colours of the boxes,
how code and outputs are shown, how to read a reference) are collected in
[How to study with this book](how-to-study.qmd). Read it once before starting.

## Software versions {.unnumbered}

All Python code was executed with **Python 3.13**; the C and C++ code of Part II
was compiled with **GCC 13** (`g++ -std=c++20`, `gcc -std=c17`) and run on
x86-64 Linux; the machine-learning code of Part III uses **scikit-learn 1.9**
with NumPy, pandas and Matplotlib (exact versions on the part's overview page). The outputs you see under each code cell were produced by
actually running that code when the book was built: they are not typed by
hand.

## Independence and licence {.unnumbered}

This is an **independent, personal work**. It is not affiliated with, endorsed
by or produced on behalf of the institution that runs the master, and it does
**not reproduce any of its course material** (lectures, slides, texts or
project assignments): the master only determined *which topics* each part
covers and in which order. The text, the examples, the proofs, the code and the
project specifications are original work written for this handbook; the
primary sources each section draws on are cited in place. All rights
reserved.

::: {.callout-note}
## A living book
The handbook is released incrementally, one course at a time. Chapters may be
refined after publication; the date at the top of each page is the date of the
last build.
:::
